title: Rebuilding a run from its events
intro: One call is left in 6A: how the rebuild gap is closed (E1), and how its test is kept honest until then (E2). Everything else in 6A is built and passes.

decisions.title: How a run is rebuilt from its events
decisions.context: `run.json` is written atomically, so a crash never leaves half a file; tested, the old or the new file is always whole. It is unreadable only after disk damage or a hand edit. `Run` has 18 fields and a rebuild must restore 16 of them (heartbeat and signals are recomputed). The catalogue's 38 events carry no fields today.

options.name: Add one event, `run_snapshot`, written after each change and carrying the whole run; rebuild replays the last one
pros: One new event and one rule; rebuild is a few lines and cannot miss a field when `Run` gains one
Measured: a mid-run snapshot is 1.8 KB, so 200 changes add about 356 KiB to `events.jsonl`
Needs no change to the other 38 events or to the modules that write them
The test already states the requirement; when the fix lands the strict marker makes the suite fail until the marker is removed (checked with pytest), so the gap cannot be closed silently
cons: Events.jsonl grows faster; the dashboard and `read_events` readers must skip or ignore snapshots
The history is a series of full states, not a story of what changed; a reader wanting 'what changed' must diff two snapshots
A snapshot can hold a value that was wrong when written, so a rebuild reproduces the wrong value

options.name: Make every catalogue event carry the fields it changes, and rebuild by replaying them
pros: No extra event and a smaller log: only the changed fields are written
The log reads as a story, which suits the dashboard's run history and audits
cons: A large spec edit: about 38 events each need a field list, across modules 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 14
Every future change to `Run` or to a module's state must also change an event, or the rebuild silently drifts
Rebuild is replay logic that must be correct for 16 fields in every order of events, and is easy to get subtly wrong

options.name: Keep the previous `run.json` as `run.json.bak` on each write; `recover --rebuild` restores it and closes open attempts
pros: Smallest change: one copy per write, no new event, no change to the catalogue
Covers the case that can actually happen, a damaged or hand-edited `run.json`, because atomic writes already stop crashes from corrupting it
cons: The backup is one write behind, so a rebuild can lose the last change and must be reconciled with the events
Does not satisfy module 6A's wording: 'from events', 'the same status, stages, loops and attention'
If both files are damaged, nothing can be rebuilt

decisions.why: One snapshot event is the smallest change that meets 6A as written, and its cost is measured at under 400 KiB for a long run.

decisions.title: How the expected failure is closed
decisions.context: The rebuild criterion is an expected failure today, marked strict. Once E1 lands, the test passes and the marker must be removed in the same change.

options.name: Keep the strict marker until the fix lands, then remove it in the same change
pros: A fix that changes the result is noticed at once
The gap stays visible in every test run until closed
cons: The fix's author must remove the marker, or the suite fails

options.name: Skip the test with a reason until the fix lands
pros: Nothing fails while the gap is open
cons: A skipped test can stay skipped for ever
The gap disappears from the test run

decisions.why: A strict expected failure keeps the gap visible and forces the marker to be removed with the fix.
